subtitle: When the real system is too costly, too slow or too dangerous to try, build a model and run that instead.

sys.body:
Would you crash a real aeroplane to learn how it behaves in a storm? Of course not. You would build a copy, a simpler version that behaves in the ways you care about, and crash that. That is the heart of simulation, and here are the words you need.

A system is a set of entities interacting toward a goal, inside an environment. A model is a simplified representation of it. Simulation is running the model over time to see how the system behaves. Systems are continuous (state changes smoothly: a tank filling) or discrete (state changes at events: customers arriving). Models may be static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic. A bank queue, where things change when customers arrive and leave, is best modelled as a discrete system.
keynotes: A system is a set of entities interacting toward a goal inside an environment; a model is a simplified representation; simulation is running the model over time.
Systems are continuous (state changes smoothly, like a tank filling) or discrete (state changes at events, like customers arriving).
Models may be static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic.

why.body:
When is it worth building a model? You simulate when experimenting on the real system is expensive, dangerous or impossible, when an analytic solution does not exist, or to compare designs cheaply. The advantages are what-if experiments, time compression and insight. The disadvantages: it needs skill and data, the results are estimates not proofs, and it can be costly to build.

A careful study follows a path, and you should walk it in order: formulate the problem → set objectives → conceptual model → collect data → translate to a program → verify → validate → design experiments → run → analyse → document. Look at the figure: two loops go back, verification and validation. In a simulation study, validation asks whether the model is the right model, one that matches the real system.
keynotes: Simulate when experimenting on the real system is expensive, dangerous or impossible, when no analytic solution exists, or to compare designs cheaply.
Advantages are what-if experiments, time compression and insight; disadvantages are needing skill and data, estimates rather than proofs, and cost.
A study runs from formulating the problem to documentation, with two loops back for verification and validation.

mc.body:
Here is a delightful trick: you can find the value of π by throwing darts. Monte Carlo uses random sampling to estimate a quantity. Throw random points at the unit square; the fraction that lands inside the quarter-circle x² + y² ≤ 1 estimates its area π/4. In the figure, green points fell inside the arc and red outside.

Try it. Out of 1000 random points, 786 fall inside the quarter circle, so π ≈ 4 × 786/1000 = 3.144. With 5000 points the estimate is 3.18 (error 0.0384). The error shrinks like 1/√n: a hundred times more points for ten times the accuracy. That is slow, but it works for problems (high-dimensional integrals, risk) where nothing else does. To make an estimate 10× more accurate you need about 100× more points.

786 of 1000 points inside gives π ≈ 3.144; with 5000 points the estimate is 3.18 (error 0.0384).

des.body:
Think of a diary with appointments in time order. You do not live through every empty minute; you jump from one appointment to the next. A discrete-event simulator works exactly like that. It keeps a clock and an ordered future event list. The loop is: take the earliest event, advance the clock to its time, update the state (and statistics), and schedule any new events it causes.

Nothing happens between events, so the clock skips over idle time. Arrivals, service completions and breakdowns are typical events. This event loop is the heart of every discrete-event simulator, as the figure shows. Between two events, the simulation clock does not advance at all; it jumps from one to the next.
keynotes: A discrete-event simulator keeps a clock and an ordered future event list.
The loop takes the earliest event, advances the clock to its time, updates the state and statistics, and schedules new events.
Nothing happens between events, so the clock skips over idle time.

mcdes.body:
You now have two big tools, and a fair question is which one to pick. Monte Carlo typically has no notion of time: each trial is independent (estimating π, or the chance a project overruns). Discrete-event simulation tracks a system’s evolution in time (queues, factories, networks).

The two are cousins, and many studies combine them: DES with random inter-arrival and service times is Monte Carlo over a dynamic model. So the one that is typically time-independent is Monte Carlo.
keynotes: Monte Carlo typically has no notion of time: each trial is independent.
Discrete-event simulation tracks a system’s evolution in time, such as queues, factories and networks.
DES with random inter-arrival and service times is Monte Carlo over a dynamic model.

summary.body:
Two lines, and you are set for the chapters ahead.

  • Model → run → analyse; verify and validate.
  • Monte Carlo: error ∝ 1/√n. DES: clock jumps between events.
keynotes: Build the model, run it, analyse it, and always verify and validate.
Monte Carlo error falls like 1/√n; in DES the clock jumps between events.
